subject: About the way to use "node" in configureMCMC

messages.author: 01ee9baab3340811
messages.subject: About the way to use "node" in configureMCMC
parts:
Hi there!

I start using nimble and I want to use Particle filter MCMC.
I have just a basic question about "node", the argument of configureMCMC().

I've already read help(configureMCMC) and the manual of MCMC(https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-mcmc.html).
However, I didn't get to understand it well. 

I tried 8.1.2 in manual(https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-algos-provided.html#particle-filters-sequential-monte-carlo-and-iterated-filtering) as a trial.
This is the code I tried

timeConf <- configureMCMC(rTimeModel, nodes = c('x[1]', 'x[3]')) # empty MCMC configuration
#timeConf <- configureMCMC(rTimeModel, nodes = NULL) 

# Add random walk PMCMC sampler with particle number optimization.
timeConf$addSampler(target = c("a", "b", "c", "mu_0"), type = "RW_PF_block",
                    control = list(propCov= diag(4), adaptScaleOnly = FALSE,adaptInterval = 1,
                                   latents = "x", pfOptimizeNparticles = FALSE, pfNparticles = 10))

cTimeModel <- compileNimble(rTimeModel)
TimeConf <- buildMCMC(timeConf)
cTimeConf <- compileNimble(TimeConf)
ressult = runMCMC(cTimeConf, niter = 1000, nchains = 1, nburnin = 100) 

I changed nodes from NULL to c('x[1]', 'x[3]') in configureMCMC, but there is no change in result.

What is the node?  How node change the calculation and result??

I'm sorry for the easy and basic question because I'm just beginner for nimble.

Best regards, 
kei

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: About the way to use "node" in configureMCMC
parts:
Dear Kei,
Thanks for posting the question and welcome to nimble.
I am not quite sure what to address. The "nodes" argument to configureMCMC tells it what nodes (parameters to be estimated) you want to have MCMC samplers assigned to. In the example, nodes=NULL creates an empty configuration, to which the PMCMC sampler (RW_PF_block) is then manually added because it is not one of the default samplers. In the example for PMCMC, I'm not sure it would really make sense to assign MCMC samplers to x[1] and x[3], because those are going to handled by the particle filter.
I'm not clear if you got a result that you didn't think was correct?

Also here is a paper with more explanation and examples about these methods in nimble and nimbleSMC. If you're in need of a firmer start, I would recommend this as it does give some general introduction to nimble prior to describing the sequential Monte Carlo algorithms.

Michaud N, De Valpine P, Turek D, Paciorek CJ, Nguyen D (2021). “Sequential Monte Carlo Methods in the nimble and nimbleSMC R Packages.” Journal of Statistical Software, 100(3), 1–39. doi:10.18637/jss.v100.i03.

I guess we should refer to this paper from the nimble user manual (although that refers to nimbleSMC, which refers to this paper).

HTH
Perry

Thank you for your fast reply!

I'm so sorry, I couldn't follow some points. I want to ask 3 questions.

Is it correct?

So I initially set the node to null, but then I define the latent in addSampler, so I am doing a particle filter with that latent as the node('x')?
Is it correct?

3. If the second question is correct, it is not necessarily to set the node in configureMCMC at first.
Is it correct?

Do these question makes sense?
If I do misunderstand, please teach me...

Thanks,
kei

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: About the way to use "node" in configureMCMC
parts:
Dear Kei,
The MCMC algorithm is an object that uses the model object. So the nodes with samplers in the MCMC are unrelated to whether you can calculate some or all parts of the model. The PMCMC example as given should work. That has nodes=NULL to create an empty MCMC configuration, so that the PMCMC sampler can be added to it. The PMCMC sampler (RW_PF_block) manages the x nodes using a particle filter. If you haven't had a chance, I would recommend gaining the basic concepts of nimble models and MCMC algorithms by working through the first parts of the nimble user manual at r-nimble.org, looking at the examples also at r-nimble.org, and also looking at some of the workshop materials available on our nimble-training GitHub organization. The nimble-virtual-2023 and nimble-lisbon-2022 were both 3-day workshops, so they have somewhat more thorough modules than the shorter workshops.
HTH
Perry
